entries.5e824984edefd843c124bf709de7a683de67c4b2: <div sID="gen1604" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Exod.9" sID="Exod.9"/> <div eID="gen1604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1605" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1606" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have an account of three more of the plagues of Egypt. I. Murrain among the cattle, which was fatal to them, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.1-Exod.9.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. Boils upon man and beast, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.8-Exod.9.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. III. Hail, with thunder and lightning. 1. Warning is given of this plague, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.13-Exod.9.21">ver. 13-21</reference>. 2. It is inflicted, to their great terror, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.22-Exod.9.26">ver. 22-26</reference>. 3. Pharaoh, in a fright, renews his treaty with Moses, but instantly breaks his word, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.27-Exod.9.35">ver. 27</reference>, &c.
entries.2e8fe355ff7b79c6b625bd0c4b7a994e3d4d63b5: <div eID="gen1606" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1605" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Plagues of Egypt. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1607" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Go in unto Pharaoh, and tell him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of the Hebrews, Let my people go, that they may serve me. <hi type="super">2</hi> For if thou refuse to let <hi type="italic">them</hi> go, and wilt hold them still, <hi type="super">3</hi> Behold, the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is upon thy cattle which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the field, upon the horses, upon the asses, upon the camels, upon the oxen, and upon the sheep: <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> a very grievous murrain. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt: and there shall nothing die of all <hi type="italic">that is</hi> the children's of Israel. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> appointed a set time, saying, To morrow the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall do this thing in the land. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did that thing on the morrow, and all the cattle of Egypt died: but of the cattle of the children of Israel died not one. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Pharaoh sent, and, behold, there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead. And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go. <div eID="gen1607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1608" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Warning given of another plague, namely, the murrain of beasts. When Pharaoh's heart was hardened, after he had seemed to relent under the former plague, then Moses is sent to tell him there is another coming, to try what that would do towards reviving the impressions of the former plagues. Thus is the wrath of God revealed from heaven, both in his word and in his works, <hi type="italic">against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men.</hi> 1. Moses puts Pharaoh in a very fair way to prevent it: <hi type="italic">Let my people go,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.9.1">v. 1</reference>. This was still the demand. God will have Israel released; Pharaoh opposes it, and the trial is, <hi type="italic">whose word shall stand.</hi> See how jealous God is for his people. When <hi type="italic">the year of his redeemed has come,</hi> he will <hi type="italic">give Egypt for their ransom;</hi> that kingdom shall be ruined, rather than Israel shall not be delivered. See how reasonable God's demands are. Whatever he calls for, it is but <hi type="italic">his own:</hi> They are my people, therefore let them go. 2. He describes the plague that should come, if he refused, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.2-Exod.9.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">The hand of the Lord</hi> immediately, without the stretching out of Aaron's hand, <hi type="italic">is upon the cattle,</hi> many of which, some of all kinds, should die by a sort of pestilence. This was greatly to the loss of the owners: they had made Israel poor, and now God would make them poor. Note, The hand of God is to be acknowledged even in the sickness and death of cattle, or other damage sustained in them; for a <hi type="italic">sparrow falls not to the ground without our Father.</hi> 3. As an evidence of the special hand of God in it, and of his particular favour to his own people, he foretells that none of their cattle should die, though they breathed in the same air and drank of the same water with the Egyptians' cattle: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall sever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.9.4">v. 4</reference>. Note, When God's judgments are abroad, though they may fall both on the righteous and the wicked, yet God makes such a distinction that they are not the same to the one that they are to the other. See <reference osisRef="Isa.27.7">Isa. xxvii. 7</reference>. The providence of God is to be acknowledged with thankfulness in the life of the cattle, for he preserveth man and beast, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Ps. xxxvi. 6</reference>. 4. To make the warning the more remarkable, the time is fixed (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">To-morrow</hi> it shall be done. We know not what any day will bring forth, and therefore we cannot say what we will do to-morrow, but it is not so with God. <div eID="gen1608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1609" type="x-p"/> II. The plague itself inflicted. The cattle died, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, The creature is made subject to vanity by the sin of man, being liable, according to its capacity, both to serve his wickedness and to share in his punishment, as in the universal deluge. <reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Rom. viii. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">22</reference>. Pharaoh and the Egyptians sinned; but the <hi type="italic">sheep, what had they done?</hi> Yet they are plagued. See <reference osisRef="Jer.12.4">Jer. xii. 4</reference>, For the <hi type="italic">wickedness of the land, the beasts are consumed.</hi> The Egyptians afterwards, and (some think) now, worshipped their cattle; it was among them that the Israelites learned to make a god of a calf: in this therefore the plague here spoken of meets with them. Note, What we make an idol of it is just with God to remove from us, or embitter to us. See <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Isa. xix. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen1609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1610" type="x-p"/> III. The distinction put between the cattle of the Egyptians and the Israelites' cattle, according to the word of God: Not <hi type="italic">one of the cattle of the Israelites died,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.9.6-Exod.9.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Does God take care of oxen? Yes, he does; his providence extends itself to the meanest of his creatures. But it is written also for our sakes, that, trusting in God, and making him our refuge, we may not be <hi type="italic">afraid of the pestilence that walketh in darkness,</hi> no, not though <hi type="italic">thousands fall at our side,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.91.6-Ps.91.7">Ps. xci. 6, 7</reference>. Pharaoh sent to see if the cattle of the Israelites were infected, not to satisfy his conscience, but only to gratify his curiosity, or with design, by way of reprisal, to repair his own losses out of their stocks; and, having no good design in the enquiry, the report brought to him made no impression upon him, but, on the contrary, his heart was hardened. Note, To those that are wilfully blind, even those methods of conviction which are ordained to life prove a savour of death unto death.
entries.1e108a00df15f14254e46f38086dc9f795669b6b: <div eID="gen1610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1611" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses and unto Aaron, Take to you handfuls of ashes of the furnace, and let Moses sprinkle it toward the heaven in the sight of Pharaoh. <hi type="super">9</hi> And it shall become small dust in all the land of Egypt, and shall be a boil breaking forth <hi type="italic">with</hi> blains upon man, and upon beast, throughout all the land of Egypt. 10 And they took ashes of the furnace, and stood before Pharaoh; and Moses sprinkled it up toward heaven; and it became a boil breaking forth <hi type="italic">with</hi> blains upon man, and upon beast. 11 And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians, and upon all the Egyptians. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he hearkened not unto them; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had spoken unto Moses. <div eID="gen1611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1612" type="x-p"/> Observe here, concerning the plague of boils and blains, <div eID="gen1612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1613" type="x-p"/> I. When they were not wrought upon by the death of their cattle, God sent a plague that seized their own bodies, and touched them to the quick. If less judgments do not do their work, God will send greater. Let us therefore humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, and go forth to meet him in the way of his judgments, that his anger may be turned away from us. <div eID="gen1613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1614" type="x-p"/> II. The signal by which this plague was summoned was the sprinkling of warm ashes from the <hi type="italic">furnace, towards heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.10">10</reference>), which was to signify the heating of the air with such an infection as should produce in the bodies of the Egyptians sore boils, which would be both noisome and painful. Immediately upon the scattering of the ashes, a scalding dew came down out of the air, which blistered wherever it fell. Note, Sometimes God shows men their sin in their punishment; they had oppressed Israel in the furnaces, and now the ashes of the furnace are made as much a terror to them as ever their task-masters had been to the Israelites. <div eID="gen1614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1615" type="x-p"/> III. The plague itself was very grievous—a common eruption would be so, especially to the nice and delicate, but these eruptions were inflammations, like Job's. This is afterwards called the <hi type="italic">botch of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.27">Deut. xxviii. 27</reference>), as if it were some new disease, never heard of before, and known ever after by that name, Note, Sores in the body are to be looked upon as the punishments of sin, and to be hearkened to as calls to repentance. <div eID="gen1615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1616" type="x-p"/> IV. The magicians themselves were struck with these boils, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.11">v. 11</reference>. 1. Thus they were punished, (1.) For helping to harden Pharaoh's heart, as Elymas for seeking to <hi type="italic">pervert the right ways of the Lord;</hi> God will severely reckon with those that strengthen the hands of the wicked in their wickedness. (2.) For pretending to imitate the former plagues, and making themselves and Pharaoh sport with them. Those that would produce lice shall, against their wills, produce boils. Note, It is ill jesting with God's judgments, and more dangerous than playing with fire. <hi type="italic">Be you not mockers, lest your bands be made strong.</hi> 2. Thus they were shamed in the presence of their admirers. How weak were their enchantments, which could not so much as secure themselves! The devil can give no protection to those that are in confederacy with him. 3. Thus they were driven from the field. Their power was restrained before (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.18">ch. viii. 18</reference>), but they continued to confront Moses, and confirm Pharaoh in his unbelief, till now, at length, they were forced to retreat, and could not stand before Moses, to which the apostle refers (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.9">2 Tim. iii. 9</reference>) when he says that their <hi type="italic">folly was made manifest unto all men.</hi> <div eID="gen1616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1617" type="x-p"/> V. Pharaoh continued obstinate, for now <hi type="italic">the Lord hardened</hi> his heart, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.12">v. 12</reference>. Before, he had hardened his own heart, and resisted the grace of God; and now God justly gave him up to his own heart's lusts, to a reprobate mind, and strong delusions, permitting Satan to blind and harden him, and ordering every thing, henceforward, so as to make him more and more obstinate. Note, Wilful hardness is commonly punished with judicial hardness. If men shut their eyes against the light, it is just with God to close their eyes. Let us dread this as the sorest judgment a man can be under on this side hell.
entries.da03d08a32125237107827ceedd59490d7702652: <div eID="gen1617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1618" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Rise up early in the morning, and stand before Pharaoh, and say unto him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of the Hebrews, Let my people go, that they may serve me. <hi type="super">14</hi> For I will at this time send all my plagues upon thine heart, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people; that thou mayest know that <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none like me in all the earth. <hi type="super">15</hi> For now I will stretch out my hand, that I may smite thee and thy people with pestilence; and thou shalt be cut off from the earth. <hi type="super">16</hi> And in very deed for this <hi type="italic">cause</hi> have I raised thee up, for to show <hi type="italic">in</hi> thee my power; and that my name may be declared throughout all the earth. 17 As yet exaltest thou thyself against my people, that thou wilt not let them go? <hi type="super">18</hi> Behold, to morrow about this time I will cause it to rain a very grievous hail, such as hath not been in Egypt since the foundation thereof even until now. <hi type="super">19</hi> Send therefore now, <hi type="italic">and</hi> gather thy cattle, and all that thou hast in the field; <hi type="italic">for upon</hi> every man and beast which shall be found in the field, and shall not be brought home, the hail shall come down upon them, and they shall die. <hi type="super">20</hi> He that feared the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> among the servants of Pharaoh made his servants and his cattle flee into the houses: <hi type="super">21</hi> And he that regarded not the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> left his servants and his cattle in the field. <div eID="gen1618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1619" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general declaration of the wrath of God against Pharaoh for his obstinacy. Though God has hardened his heart (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.12">v. 12</reference>), yet Moses must repeat his applications to him; God suspends his grace and yet demands obedience, to punish him for requiring bricks of the children of Israel when he denied them straw. God would likewise show forth a pattern of long-suffering, and how he waits to be gracious to a <hi type="italic">rebellious and gainsaying people</hi> Six times the demand had been made in vain, yet Moses must make it the seventh time: <hi type="italic">Let my people go,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.9.13">v. 13</reference>. A most dreadful message Moses is here ordered to deliver to him, whether he will hear or whether he will forbear. 1. He must tell him that he is marked for ruin, that he now stands as the butt at which God would shoot all the arrows of his wrath, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.14-Exod.9.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. "Now I will send <hi type="italic">all my plagues.</hi>" Now that no place is found for repentance in Pharaoh, nothing can prevent his utter destruction, for that only would have prevented it. Now that God begins to <hi type="italic">harden his heart,</hi> his case is desperate. "I will send my plagues <hi type="italic">upon thy heart,</hi> not only temporal plagues upon thy body, but spiritual plagues upon thy soul." Note, God can send plagues upon thy soul." Note, God can send plagues upon the heart, either by making it senseless or by making it hopeless—and these are the worst plagues. Pharaoh must now expect no respite, no cessation of arms, but to be followed with plague upon plague, till he is utterly consumed. Note, When God judges he will overcome; none ever hardened his heart against him and prospered. 2. He must tell him that he is to remain in history a standing monument of the justice and power of God's wrath (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For this cause have I raised thee up</hi> to the throne at this time, and made thee to stand the shock of the plagues hitherto, to <hi type="italic">show in thee my power.</hi>" Providence ordered it so that Moses should have a man of such a fierce and stubborn spirit as he was to deal with; and every thing was so managed in this transaction as to make it a most signal and memorable instance of the power God has to humble and bring down the proudest of his enemies. Every thing concurred to signalize this, that God's name (that is, his incontestable sovereignty, his irresistible power, and his inflexible justice) might be declared throughout all the earth, not only to all places, but through all ages while the earth remains. Note, God sometimes raises up very bad men to honour and power, spares them long, and suffers them to grow insufferably insolent, that he may be so much the more glorified in their destruction at last. See how the neighbouring nations, at that time, improved the ruin of Pharaoh to the glory of God. Jethro said upon it, <hi type="italic">Now know I that the Lord is greater than all gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.18.11">ch. xviii. 11</reference>. The apostle illustrates the doctrine of God's sovereignty with this instance, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.17">Rom. ix. 17</reference>. To justify God in these resolutions, Moses is directed to ask him (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">As yet exaltest thou thyself against my people?</hi> Pharaoh was a great king; God's people were poor shepherds at the best, and now poor slaves; and yet Pharaoh shall be ruined if he exalt himself against them, for it is considered as exalting himself against God. This was not the first time that God reproved kings for their sakes, and let them know that he would not suffer his people to be trampled upon and insulted, no, not by the most powerful of them. <div eID="gen1619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1620" type="x-p"/> II. A particular prediction of the plague of hail (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.18">v. 18</reference>), and a gracious advice to Pharaoh and his people to send for their servants and cattle out of the field, that they might be sheltered from the hail, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.19">v. 19</reference>. Note, When God's justice threatens ruin his mercy, at the same time, shows us a way of escape from it, so unwilling is he that any should perish. See here what care God took, not only to distinguish between Egyptians and Israelites, but between some Egyptians and others. If Pharaoh will not yield, and so prevent the judgment itself, yet an opportunity is given to those that have any dread of God and his word to save themselves from sharing in the judgment. Note, Those that will take warning may take shelter; and those that will not may thank themselves if they fall by the overflowing scourge, and the hail which will <hi type="italic">sweep away the refuge of lies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Isa. xxviii. 17</reference>. See the different effect of this warning. 1. <hi type="italic">Some believed the things that were spoken,</hi> and they feared, and housed their servants and cattle (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.20">v. 20)</reference>, like Noah (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.7">Heb. xi. 7</reference>), and it was their wisdom. Even among the servants of Pharaoh there were some that trembled at God's word; and shall not the sons of Israel dread it? But, 2. Others believed not: though, whatever plague Moses had hitherto foretold, the event exactly answered to the prediction; and though, if they had had any reason to question this, it would have been no great damage to them to have kept their cattle in the house for one day, and so, supposing it a doubtful case, to have chosen the surer side; yet they were so foolhardy as in defiance to the truth of Moses, and the power of God (of both which they had already had experience enough, to their cost), to leave their cattle in the field, Pharaoh himself, it is probable, giving them an example of the presumption, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.21">v. 21</reference>. Note, Obstinate infidelity, which is deaf to the fairest warnings and the wisest counsels, leaves the blood of those that perish upon their own heads.
entries.6ed9643db8bcd9c4250e0f5f60fba91311e29447: <div eID="gen1620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1621" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Stretch forth thine hand toward heaven, that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, upon man, and upon beast, and upon every herb of the field, throughout the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">23</hi> And Moses stretched forth his rod toward heaven: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> rained hail upon the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">24</hi> So there was hail, and fire mingled with the hail, very grievous, such as there was none like it in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the hail smote throughout all the land of Egypt all that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the field, both man and beast; and the hail smote every herb of the field, and brake every tree of the field. <hi type="super">26</hi> Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel <hi type="italic">were,</hi> was there no hail. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Pharaoh sent, and called for Moses and Aaron, and said unto them, I have sinned this time: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> righteous, and I and my people <hi type="italic">are</hi> wicked. <hi type="super">28</hi> Intreat the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> (for <hi type="italic">it is</hi> enough) that there be no <hi type="italic">more</hi> mighty thunderings and hail; and I will let you go, and ye shall stay no longer. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Moses said unto him, As soon as I am gone out of the city, I will spread abroad my hands unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="italic">and</hi> the thunder shall cease, neither shall there be any more hail; that thou mayest know how that the earth <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's. <hi type="super">30</hi> But as for thee and thy servants, I know that ye will not yet fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God. <hi type="super">31</hi> And the flax and the barley was smitten: for the barley <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the ear, and the flax <hi type="italic">was</hi> bolled. <hi type="super">32</hi> But the wheat and the rye were not smitten: for they <hi type="italic">were</hi> not grown up. <hi type="super">33</hi> And Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh, and spread abroad his hands unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and the thunders and hail ceased, and the rain was not poured upon the earth. <hi type="super">34</hi> And when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunders were ceased, he sinned yet more, and hardened his heart, he and his servants. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, neither would he let the children of Israel go; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had spoken by Moses. <div eID="gen1621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1622" type="x-p"/> The threatened plague of hail is here summoned by the powerful hand and rod of Moses (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.22-Exod.9.23">v. 22, 23</reference>), and it obeys the summons, or rather the divine command; for <hi type="italic">fire and hail fulfil God's word,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.148.8">Ps. cxlviii. 8</reference>. And here we are told, <div eID="gen1622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1623" type="x-p"/> I. What desolations it made upon the earth. The thunder, and fire from heaven (or lightning), made it both the more dreadful and the more destroying, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.23-Exod.9.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. Note, God makes the clouds, not only his store-houses whence he drops fatness on his people, but his magazines whence, when he pleases, he can draw out a most formidable train of artillery, with which to destroy his enemies. He himself speaks of the <hi type="italic">treasures of hail which he hath reserved against the day of battle and war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.22-Job.38.23">Job xxxviii. 22, 23</reference>. Woeful havoc this hail made in the land of Egypt. It killed both men and cattle, and battered down, not only the herbs, but the trees, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.25">v. 25</reference>. The corn that was above ground was destroyed, and that only preserved which as yet had not come up, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.31-Exod.9.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. Note, God has many ways of <hi type="italic">taking away the corn in the season thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.9">Hos. ii. 9</reference>), either by a secret blasting, or a noisy hail. In this plague the <hi type="italic">hot thunderbolts,</hi> as well as the hail, are said to destroy <hi type="italic">their flocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.47-Ps.78.48">Ps. lxxviii. 47, 48</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Ps.105.32-Ps.105.33">Ps. cv. 32, 33</reference>. Perhaps David alludes to this when, describing God's glorious appearances for the discomfiture of his enemies, he speaks of the hailstones and coals of fire he threw among them, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12-Ps.18.13">Ps. xviii. 12, 13</reference>. And there is a plan reference to it on the pouring out of the seventh vial, <reference osisRef="Rev.16.21">Rev. xvi. 21</reference>. Notice is here taken (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.26">v. 26</reference>) of the land of Goshen's being preserved from receiving any damage by this plague. God has the directing of the pregnant clouds, and causes it to rain or hail on one city and not on another, either in mercy or in judgment. <div eID="gen1623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1624" type="x-p"/> II. What a consternation it put Pharaoh in. See what effect it had upon him, 1. He humbled himself to Moses in the language of a penitent, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.27-Exod.9.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. No man could have spoken better. He owns himself on the wrong side in his contest with the God of the Hebrews: "<hi type="italic">I have sinned</hi> in standing it out so long." He owns the equity of God's proceedings against him: <hi type="italic">The Lord is righteous,</hi> and must be justified when he speaks, though he speak in thunder and lightning. He condemns himself and his land: "<hi type="italic">I and my people are wicked,</hi> and deserve what is brought upon us." He begs the prayers of Moses: "<hi type="italic">Entreat the Lord</hi> for me, that this direful plague may be removed." And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> he promises to yield up his prisoners: <hi type="italic">I will let you go.</hi> What could one desire more? And yet his heart was hardened all this while. Note, The terror of the rod often extorts penitent acknowledgments from those who have no penitent affections; under the surprise and smart of affliction, they start up, and say that which is pertinent enough, not because they are deeply affected, but because they know that they should be and that <hi type="italic">it is meet to be said.</hi> 2. Moses, hereupon, becomes an intercessor for him with God. Though he had all the reason in the world to think that he would immediately repent of his repentance, and told him so (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.30">v. 30</reference>), yet he promises to be this friend in the court of heaven. Note, Even those whom we have little hopes of, yet we should continue to pray for, and to admonish, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.23">1 Sam. xii. 23</reference>. Observe, (1.) The place Moses chose for his intercession. He went <hi type="italic">out of the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.33">v. 33</reference>), not only for privacy in his communion with God, but to show that he durst venture abroad into the field, notwithstanding the hail and lightning which kept Pharaoh and his servants withindoors, knowing that every hail-stone had its direction from his God, who meant him no hurt. Note, Peace with God makes men thunderproof, for thunder is the voice of their Father. (2.) The gesture: He <hi type="italic">spread abroad his hands unto the Lord</hi>—an outward expression of earnest desire and humble expectation. Those that come to God for mercy must stand ready to receive it. (3.) The end Moses aimed at in interceding for him: <hi type="italic">That thou mayest know,</hi> and be convinced, <hi type="italic">that the earth is the Lord's</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.29">v. 29</reference>), that is, that God has a sovereign dominion over all the creatures, that they all are ruled by him, and therefore that thou oughtest to be so. See what various methods God uses to bring men to their proper senses. Judgments are sent, judgments removed, and all for the same end, to make men know that he Lord reigns. (4.) The success of it. [1.] He prevailed with God, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.33">v. 33</reference>. But, [2.] He could not prevail with Pharaoh: <hi type="italic">He sinned yet more, and hardened his heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.9.34-Exod.9.35">v. 34, 35</reference>. The prayer of Moses opened and shut heaven, like Elias's (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.17-Jas.5.18">Jam. v. 17, 18</reference>), and such is the power of God's two witnesses (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.6">Rev. xi. 6</reference>); yet neither Moses nor Elias, nor those two witnesses, could subdue the hard hearts of men. Pharaoh was frightened into a compliance by the judgment, but, when it was over, his convictions vanished, and his fair promises were forgotten. Note, Little credit is to be given to confessions upon the rack. Note also, Those that are not bettered by judgments and mercies are commonly made worse.  <chapter eID="Exod.9"/> <div eID="gen1624" type="x-p"/>

entries.d1305386bfe2512d387360718815638d821f809e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv661"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.9.1-Exod.9.7">Ex 9:1-7</reference>. Murrain of Beasts.</title> <div sID="gen940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv661"/><hi type="bold">3-5. Behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thy cattle--</hi>A fifth application was made to Pharaoh in behalf of the Israelites by Moses, who was instructed to tell him that, if he persisted in opposing their departure, a pestilence would be sent among all the flocks and herds of the Egyptians, while those of the Israelites would be spared. As he showed no intention of keeping his promise, he was still a mark for the arrows of the Almighty's quiver, and the threatened plague of which he was forewarned was executed. But it is observable that in this instance it was not inflicted through the instrumentality or waving of Aaron's rod, but directly by the hand of the Lord, and the fixing of the precise time tended still further to determine the true character of the calamity (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.4">Jr 12:4</reference>). <div eID="gen940" type="x-p"/>
entries.5cbf9952066242275c082d373cab56149641f24e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv662"/><div sID="gen941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv662"/><hi type="bold">6. all the cattle of Egypt died--</hi>not absolutely every beast, for we find (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.19">Ex 9:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.21">21</reference>) that there were still some left; but a great many died of each herd--the mortality was frequent and widespread. The adaptation of this judgment consisted in Egyptians venerating the more useful animals such as the ox, the cow, and the ram; in all parts of the country temples were reared and divine honors paid to these domesticated beasts, and thus while the pestilence caused a great loss in money, it also struck a heavy blow at their superstition. <div eID="gen941" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8fb8cce9b6fa7145344bc93db0e526c9c55d71a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv663"/><div sID="gen942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv663"/><hi type="bold">7. Pharaoh sent ... there was not one of the cattle of the Israelites dead--</hi>The despatch of confidential messengers indicates that he would not give credit to vague reports, and we may conclude that some impression had been made on his mind by that extraordinary exemption, but it was neither a good nor a permanent impression. His pride and obstinacy were in no degree subdued. <div eID="gen942" type="x-p"/>
entries.a02dea94e9a964e4ee774a6099c8f174af1aa682: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv664"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.9.8-Exod.9.17">Ex 9:8-17</reference>. Plague of Boils.</title> <div sID="gen943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv664"/><hi type="bold">8. Take to you handfuls of ashes, &c.--</hi>The next plague assailed the persons of the Egyptians, and it appeared in the form of ulcerous eruptions upon the skin and flesh (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.20">Le 13:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.7">2Ki 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.7">Job 2:7</reference>). That this epidemic did not arise from natural causes was evident from its taking effect from the particular action of Moses done in the sight of Pharaoh. The attitude he assumed was similar to that of Eastern magicians, who, "when they pronounce an imprecation on an individual, a village, or a country, take the ashes of cows' dung (that is, from a common fire) and throw them in the air, saying to the objects of their displeasure, such a sickness or such a curse shall come upon you" [Roberts]. <div eID="gen943" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea4ebdc22aeb72a724f6f612dc4e7acea69b8d86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv665"/><div sID="gen944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv665"/><hi type="bold">10. Moses took ashes from the furnace--</hi>Hebrew, "brick-kiln." The magicians, being sufferers in their own persons, could do nothing, though they had been called; and as the brick-kiln was one of the principal instruments of oppression to the Israelites [De 4:20; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.51">1Ki 8:51</reference>; Jr 11:4], it was now converted into a means of chastisement to the Egyptians, who were made to read their sin in their punishment. <div eID="gen944" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcb592e19ef0f5f55ea795f89eb2e824ef11e5b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv666"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.9.18-Exod.9.35">Ex 9:18-35</reference>. Plague of Hail.</title> <div sID="gen945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv666"/><hi type="bold">18. I will cause it to rain a very grievous hail, &c.--</hi>The seventh plague which Pharaoh's hardened heart provoked was that of hail, a phenomenon which must have produced the greatest astonishment and consternation in Egypt as rain and hailstones, accompanied by thunder and lightning, were very rare occurrences.<div eID="gen945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">such as hath not been in Egypt--</hi>In the Delta, or lower Egypt, where the scene is laid, rain occasionally falls between January and March--hail is not unknown, and thunder sometimes heard. But a storm, not only exhibiting all these elements, but so terrific that hailstones of immense size fell, thunder pealed in awful volleys, and lightning swept the ground like fire, was an unexampled calamity. <div eID="gen946" type="x-p"/>
entries.58e41c5d09e45809536e2b6ee5ddf80d7055805c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv667"/><div sID="gen947" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv667"/><hi type="bold">20-21. He that feared the word of the Lord ... regarded not, &c.--</hi>Due premonition, it appears, had been publicly given of the impending tempest--the cattle seem to have been sent out to graze, which is from January to April, when alone pasturage can be obtained, and accordingly the cattle were in the fields. This storm occurring at that season, not only struck universal terror into the minds of the people, but occasioned the destruction of all--people and cattle--which, in neglect of the warning, had been left in the fields, as well as of all vegetation [Ex 9:25]. It was the more appalling because hailstones in Egypt are small and of little force; lightning also is scarcely ever known to produce fatal effects; and to enhance the wonder, not a trace of any storm was found in Goshen [Ex 9:26]. <div eID="gen947" type="x-p"/>
entries.098e78366e4efb910a31fc8bb883aa6fafaf6c76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv668"/><div sID="gen948" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv668"/><hi type="bold">27-35. Pharaoh sent, and called for Moses and Aaron, and said unto them, I have sinned--</hi>This awful display of divine displeasure did seriously impress the mind of Pharaoh, and, under the weight of his convictions, he humbles himself to confess he has done wrong in opposing the divine will. At the same time he calls for Moses to intercede for cessation of the calamity. Moses accedes to his earnest wishes, and this most awful visitation ended. But his repentance proved a transient feeling, and his obduracy soon became as great as before. <div eID="gen948" type="x-p"/>

entries.385df35d74d1b4ec540f93d8b74cd9c7b0b3a623: <div eID="gen2662" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen2663" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2664" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2664" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2663" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2665" type="x-p"/> The Lord sends Moses to Pharaoh to inform him that, if he did not let the Israelites depart, a destructive pestilence should be sent among his cattle, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.1-Exo.9.3">Exo 9:1-3</reference>; while the cattle of the Israelites should be preserved, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.4">Exo 9:4</reference>. The next day this pestilence, which was the fifth plague, is sent, and all the cattle of the Egyptians die, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.5">Exo 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.6">Exo 9:6</reference>. Though Pharaoh finds that not one of the cattle of the Israelites had died, yet, through hardness of heart, he refuses to let the people go, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.7">Exo 9:7</reference>. Moses and Aaron are commanded to sprinkle handfuls of ashes from the furnace, that the sixth plague, that of boils and blains, might come on man and beast, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.5">Exo 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.9">Exo 9:9</reference>; which having done, the plague takes place, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.10">Exo 9:10</reference>. The magicians cannot stand before this plague, which they can neither imitate nor remove, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.11">Exo 9:11</reference>. Pharaoh's heart is again hardened, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.12">Exo 9:12</reference>. God's awful message to Pharaoh, with the threat of more severe plagues than before, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.13-Exo.9.17">Exo 9:13-17</reference>. The seventh plague of rain, hail, and fire threatened, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.18">Exo 9:18</reference>. The Egyptians commanded to house their cattle that they might not be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.19">Exo 9:19</reference>. These who feared the word of the Lord brought home their servants and cattle, and those who did not regard that word left their cattle and servants in the fields, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.20">Exo 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.21">Exo 9:21</reference>. The storm of hail, thunder, and lightning takes place, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.22-Exo.9.24">Exo 9:22-24</reference>. It nearly desolates the whole land of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.25">Exo 9:25</reference>, while the land of Goshen escapes, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.26">Exo 9:26</reference>. Pharaoh confesses his sin, and begs an interest in the prayers of Moses and Aaron, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.27">Exo 9:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.28">Exo 9:28</reference>. Moses promises to intercede for him, and while he promises that the storm shall cease, he foretells the continuing obstinacy of both himself and his servants, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.29">Exo 9:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.30">Exo 9:30</reference>. The flax and barley, being in a state of maturity, are destroyed by the tempest, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.31">Exo 9:31</reference>; while the wheat and the rye, not being grown up, are preserved, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.32">Exo 9:32</reference>. Moses obtains a cessation of the storm, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.33">Exo 9:33</reference>. Pharaoh and his servants, seeing this, harden their hearts, and refuse to let the people go, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.34">Exo 9:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.35">Exo 9:35</reference>. <div eID="gen2665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2666" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen2666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2667" type="x-p"/> The Lord God of the Hebrews - It is very likely that the term Lord, יויה Yehovah, is used here to point out particularly his eternal power and Godhead; and that the term God, אלהי Elohey, is intended to be understood in the sense of Supporter, Defender, Protector, etc. Thus saith the self-existent, omnipotent, and eternal Being, the Supporter and Defender of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may worship me."
entries.d93cd9d248228ec430a750fa83b2ed3b8516fd5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen2667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2668" type="x-p"/> The hand of the Lord - The power of God manifested in judgment. <div eID="gen2668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2669" type="x-p"/> Upon the horses - סוסים susim. This is the first place the horse is mentioned; a creature for which Egypt and Arabia were always famous. סס sus is supposed to have the same meaning with שש sas, which signifies to be active, brisk, or lively, all which are proper appellatives of the horse, especially in Arabia and Egypt. Because of their activity and swiftness they were sacrificed and dedicated to the sun, and perhaps it was principally on this account that God prohibited the use of them among the Israelites. <div eID="gen2669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2670" type="x-p"/> A very grievous murrain - The murrain is a very contagious disease among cattle, the symptoms of which are a hanging down and swelling of the head, abundance of gum in the eyes, rattling in the throat, difficulty of breathing, palpitation of the heart, staggering, a hot breath, and a shining tongue; which symptoms prove that a general inflammation has taken place. The original word דבר deber is variously translated. The Septuagint have θανατος, death; the Vulgate has pestis, a plague or pestilence; the old Saxon version, to die, any fatal disease. Our English word murrain comes either from the French mourir, to die, or from the Greek μαραινω maraino, to grow lean, waste away. The term mortality would be the nearest in sense to the original, as no particular disorder is specified by the Hebrew word.
entries.a2e758a6282ee85f03abbb130904bef0ea5d21cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen2670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2671" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall sever - See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.8.22">Exo 8:22</reference> (note).
entries.7c0b1f813a1287d168bb64a147745677f4483b6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen2671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2672" type="x-p"/> To-morrow the Lord shall do this - By thus foretelling the evil, he showed his prescience and power; and from this both the Egyptians and Hebrews must see that the mortality that ensued was no casualty, but the effect of a predetermined purpose in the Divine justice.
entries.14064b337e38b6fa52de34b4030016d455c881e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen2672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2673" type="x-p"/> All the cattle of Egypt died - That is, All the cattle that did die belonged to the Egyptians, but not one died that belonged to the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.4">Exo 9:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.6">Exo 9:6</reference>. That the whole stock of cattle belonging to the Egyptians did not die we have the fullest proof, because there were cattle both to be killed and saved alive in the ensuing plague, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.19-Exo.9.25">Exo 9:19-25</reference>. By this judgment the Egyptians must see the vanity of the whole of their national worship, when they found the animals which they not only held sacred but deified, slain without distinction among the common herd, by a pestilence sent from the hand of Jehovah. One might naturally suppose that after this the animal worship of the Egyptians could never more maintain its ground.
entries.8b74d8ecb2ab0815d453fb5f1fc1a1063003e93a: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen2673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2674" type="x-p"/> And Pharaoh sent, etc. - Finding so many of his own cattle and those of his subjects slain, he sent to see whether the mortality had reached to the cattle of the Israelites, that he might know whether this were a judgment inflicted by their God, and probably designing to replace the lost cattle of the Egyptians with those of the Israelites.
entries.2be6caaad1d4d791da82219badd092d4084d2003: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen2674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2675" type="x-p"/> Handfuls of ashes of the furnace - As one part of the oppression of the Israelites consisted In their labor in the brick-kilns, some have observed a congruity between the crime and the punishment. The furnaces, in the labor of which they oppressed the Hebrews, now yielded the instruments of their punishment; for every particle of those ashes, formed by unjust and oppressive labor, seemed to be a boil or a blain on the tyrannical king and his cruel and hard-hearted people.
entries.61274508a5c139d3dd84386ed8e509889dbe0259: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen2675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2676" type="x-p"/> Shall be a boil - שחין shechin. This word is generally expounded, an inflammatory swelling, a burning boil; one of the most poignant afflictions, not immediately mortal, that can well affect the surface of the human body. If a single boil on any part of the body throws the whole system into a fever, what anguish must a multitude of them on the body at the same time occasion! <div eID="gen2676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2677" type="x-p"/> Breaking forth with blains - אבעבעת ababuoth, supposed to come from בעה baah, to swell, bulge out; any inflammatory swelling, node, or pustule, in any part of the body, but more especially in the more glandular parts, the neck, arm-pits, groin, etc. The Septuagint translate it thus: Και εσται ἑλκη φλυκτιδες αναζεουσαι· And it shalt be an ulcer with burning pustules. It seems to have been a disorder of an uncommon kind, and hence it is called by way of distinction, the botch of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.27">Deu 28:27</reference>, perhaps never known before in that or any other country. Orosius says that in the sixth plague "all the people were blistered, that the blisters burst with tormenting pain, and that worms issued out of them." Alfred's Oros., lib. i., c. vii.
entries.66c9efecdd6cf9bb1ded33e782b5155ea3cfe49a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen2677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2678" type="x-p"/> The boil was upon the magicians - They could not produce a similar malady by throwing ashes in the air; and they could neither remove the plague from the people, nor from their own tormented flesh. Whether they perished in this plague we know not, but they are no more mentioned. If they were not destroyed by this awful judgment, they at least left the field, and no longer contended with these messengers of God. The triumph of God's power was now complete, and both the Hebrews and the Egyptians must see that there was neither might, nor wisdom, nor counsel against the Lord; and that, as universal nature acknowledged his power, devils and men must fail before him.
entries.7b14b3d263ff2758ae47dfaaa830bb5b400e4320: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen2678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2679" type="x-p"/> For now I will stretch out my hand - In the Hebrew the verbs are in the past tense, and not in the future, as our translation improperly expresses them, by which means a contradiction appears in the text: for neither Pharaoh nor his people were smitten by a pestilence, nor was he by any kind of mortality cut off from the earth. It is true the first-born were slain by a destroying angel, and Pharaoh himself was drowned in the Red Sea; but these judgments do not appear to be referred to in this place. If the words be translated, as they ought, in the subjunctive mood, or in the past instead of the future, this seeming contradiction to facts, as well as all ambiguity, will be avoided: For if now I Had Stretched Out (שלהתי shalachti, had set forth) my hand, and had smitten thee (ואך אותך vaach otheca) and thy people with the pestilence, thou Shouldst Have Been cut off (תכחד ticcached) from the earth.
entries.e0b4021d80c1fc650ac1e42a7742c98d3226c6f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen2679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2680" type="x-p"/> But truly, on this very account, have I caused thee to subsist - (העמדחיך heemadticha), that I might cause thee to see my power, (הראתך את כחי harotheca eth cochi), and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth, (or, בכל הארץ becol haarets, in all this land). See Ainsworth and Houbigant. <div eID="gen2680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2681" type="x-p"/> Thus God gave this impious king to know that it was in consequence of his especial providence that both he and his people had not been already destroyed by means of the past plagues; but God had preserved him for this very purpose, that he might have a farther opportunity of manifesting that he, Jehovah, was the only true God for the full conviction both of the Hebrews and Egyptians, that the former might follow and the latter fear before him. Judicious critics of almost all creeds have agreed to translate the original as above, a translation which it not only can bear but requires, and which is in strict conformity to both the Septuagint and Targum. Neither the Hebrew העמדחיך heemadticha, I have caused thee to stand; nor the apostle's translation of it, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.17">Rom 9:17</reference>, εξηγειρα σε, I have raised thee; nor that of the Septuagint, ἑνεκεν τουτου διετηρηθης, on this account art thou preserved, viz., in the past plagues; can countenance that most exceptionable meaning put on the words by certain commentators, viz., "That God ordained or appointed Pharaoh from all eternity, by certain means, to this end; that he made him to exist in time; that he raised him to the throne; promoted him to that high honor and dignity; that he preserved him, and did not cut him off as yet; that he strengthened and hardened his heart; irritated, provoked, and stirred him up against his people Israel, and suffered him to go all the lengths he did go in his obstinacy and rebellion; all which was done to show in him his power in destroying him in the Red Sea. The sum of which is, that this man was raised up by God in every sense for God to show his power in his destruction." So man speaks; thus God hath not spoken. See Henry on the place.
entries.995b1c0d4e5bb1766993cb034c832246433041ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen2681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2682" type="x-p"/> As yet exaltest thou thyself against my people - So it appears that at this time he might have submitted, and thus prevented his own destruction.
entries.d466790c44758f680c3a09205143da5aa5b3bf49: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen2682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2683" type="x-p"/> To-morrow about this time - The time of this plague is marked thus circumstantially to show Pharaoh that Jehovah was Lord of heaven and earth, and that the water, the fire, the earth, and the air, which were all objects of Egyptian idolatry, were the creatures of his power; and subservient to his will; and that, far from being able to help them, they were now, in the hands of God, instruments of their destruction. <div eID="gen2683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2684" type="x-p"/> To rain a very grievous hail - To rain hail may appear to some superficial observers as an unphilosophical mode of expression, but nothing can be more correct. "Drops of rain falling through a cold region of the atmosphere are frozen and converted into hail;" and thus the hail is produced by rain. When it begins to fall it is rain; when it is falling it is converted into hail; thus it is literally true that it rains hail. The farther a hail-stone falls the larger it generally is, because in its descent it meets with innumerable particles of water, which, becoming attached to it, are also frozen, and thus its bulk is continually increasing till it reaches the earth. In the case in question, if natural means were at all used, we may suppose a highly electrified state of an atmosphere loaded with vapors, which, becoming condensed and frozen, and having a considerable space to fall through, were of an unusually large size. Though this was a supernatural storm, there have been many of a natural kind, that have been exceedingly dreadful. A storm of hail fell near Liverpool, in Lancashire, in the year 1795, which greatly damaged the vegetation, broke windows, etc., etc. Many of the stones measured five inches in circumference. Dr. Halley mentions a similar storm of hail in Lancashire, Cheshire, etc., in 1697, April 29, that for sixty miles in length and two miles in breadth did immense damage, by splitting trees, killing fowls and all small animals, knocking down men and horses, etc., etc. Mezeray, in his History of France, says "that in Italy, in 1510, there was for some time a horrible darkness, thicker than that of night, after which the clouds broke into thunder and lightning, and there fell a shower of hail-stones which destroyed all the beasts, birds, and even fish of the country. It was attended with a strong smell of sulphur, and the stones were of a bluish color, some of them weighing one hundred pounds' weight." The Almighty says to Job: "Hast thou seen the treasures of the hail, which I have reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war?" <reference osisRef="Job.38.22">Job 38:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.38.23">Job 38:23</reference>. While God has such artillery at his command, how soon may he desolate a country or a world! See the account of a remarkable hail-storm in <reference osisRef="Jos.10.11">Jos 10:11</reference>.
entries.9853c81c2150a9301ca0d84284279ae997f82be4: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen2684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2685" type="x-p"/> Send - now, and gather thy cattle - So in the midst of judgment, God remembered mercy. The miracle should be wrought that they might know he was the Lord; but all the lives both of men and beasts might have been saved, had Pharaoh and his servants taken the warning so mercifully given them. While some regarded not the word of the Lord, others feared it, and their cattle and their servants were saved, See <reference osisRef="Exo.9.20">Exo 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.21">Exo 9:21</reference>.
entries.696272338171ebbfa75d9486890df962856f1a2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen2685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2686" type="x-p"/> The Lord sent thunder - קלת koloth, voices; but loud, repeated peals of thunder are meant. <div eID="gen2686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2687" type="x-p"/> And the fire ran along upon the ground - ותהלך אש ארצה vattihalac esh aretsah, and the fire walked upon the earth. It was not a sudden flash of lightning, but a devouring fire, walking through every part, destroying both animals and vegetables; and its progress was irresistible.
entries.88d217b5eb83801c81513e048b0082b3c2b68e8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen2687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2688" type="x-p"/> Hail, and fire mingled with the hail - It is generally allowed that the electric fluid is essential to the formation of hail. On this occasion it was supplied in a supernatural abundance; for streams of fire seem to have accompanied the descending hail, so that herbs and trees, beasts and men, were all destroyed by them.
entries.a0ce0afc533c3ac747b3808bdb9d3c5ec06f0580: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen2688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2689" type="x-p"/> Only in the land of Goshen - was there no hail - What a signal proof of a most particular providence! Surely both the Hebrews and Egyptians profited by this display of the goodness and severity of God.
entries.822ca88d6c1681e9668b3884db3fc45d1c5ff63c: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen2689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2690" type="x-p"/> The Lord is righteous, and I and my people are wicked - The original is very emphatic: The Lord is The Righteous One, (הצדיק hatstaddik), and I and my people are The Sinners, (הרשעים hareshaim); i.e., He is alone righteous, and we alone are transgressors. Who could have imagined that after such an acknowledgment and confession, Pharaoh should have again hardened his heart?
entries.c612e33ca448662d75b1705e42a50dcd8aedd7de: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen2690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2691" type="x-p"/> It is enough - There is no need of any farther plague; I submit to the authority of Jehovah and will rebel no more. <div eID="gen2691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2692" type="x-p"/> Mighty thunderings - כלת אלהים koloth Elohim, voices of God; - that is, superlatively loud thunder. So mountains of God (<reference osisRef="Psa.36.6">Psa 36:6</reference>) means exceeding high mountains. So a prince of God (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.6">Gen 23:6</reference>) means a mighty prince. See a description of thunder, <reference osisRef="Psa.29.3-Psa.29.8">Psa 29:3-8</reference> : "The Voice Of The Lord is upon the waters: the God of glory thundereth; the Lord is upon many waters. The voice of the Lord is powerful; the voice of the Lord is full of majesty. The voice of the Lord breaketh the cedars. The voice of the Lord divideth the flames of fire. The voice of the Lord shaketh the wilderness," etc. The production of rain by the electric spark is alluded to in a very beautiful manner, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">Jer 10:13</reference> : When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen 7:11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gen.8.1">Gen 8:1</reference> (note).
entries.4f4fcde8b69e04679d2ceeb5330766673fc93d87: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen2692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2693" type="x-p"/> I will spread abroad my hands - That is, I will make supplication to God that he may remove this plague. This may not be an improper place to make some observations on the ancient manner of approaching the Divine Being in prayer. Kneeling down, stretching out the hands, and lifting them up to heaven, were in frequent use among the Hebrews in their religious worship. Solomon kneeled down on his knees, and spread forth his hands to heaven; <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.13">2Chr 6:13</reference>. So David, <reference osisRef="Psa.143.6">Psa 143:6</reference> : I stretch forth my hands unto thee. So Ezra: I fell upon my knees, and spread out my hands unto the Lord my God; <reference osisRef="Ezr.9.5">Ezr 9:5</reference>. See also Job <reference osisRef="Job.11.13">Job 11:13</reference> : If thou prepare thine heart, and stretch out thy hands towards him. Most nations who pretended to any kind of worship made use of the same means in approaching the objects of their adoration, viz., kneeling down and stretching out their hands; which custom it is very likely they borrowed from the people of God. Kneeling was ever considered to be the proper posture of supplication, as it expresses humility, contrition, and subjection. If the person to whom the supplication was addressed was within reach, the supplicant caught him by the knees; for as among the ancients the forehead was consecrated to genius, the ear to memory, and the right hand to faith, so the knees were consecrated to mercy. Hence those who entreated favor fell at and caught hold of the knees of the person whose kindness they supplicated. This mode of supplication is particularly referred to in the following passages in Homer: - Των νυν μιν μνησασα παρεζεο, και λαβε γουνων. <div eID="gen2693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2694" type="x-p"/> Iliad i., ver. 407. <div eID="gen2694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2695" type="x-p"/> Now therefore, of these things reminding Jove, <div eID="gen2695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2696" type="x-p"/> Embrace his knees. <div eID="gen2696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2697" type="x-p"/> Cowper. <div eID="gen2697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2698" type="x-p"/> To which the following answer is made: - Και τοτ' επειτα τοι ειμι Διος ποτι χαλκοβατες δω, Και μιν γουνασομαι, και μιν πεισεσθαι οΐω. <div eID="gen2698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2699" type="x-p"/> Iliad i., ver. 426. <div eID="gen2699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2700" type="x-p"/> Then will I to Jove's brazen-floor'd abode, That I may clasp his knees; and much misdeem Of my endeavor, or my prayer shall speed. Id. See the issue of thus addressing Jove, Ibid., ver. 500-502, and ver. 511, etc. <div eID="gen2700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2701" type="x-p"/> In the same manner we find our Lord accosted, <reference osisRef="Mat.17.14">Mat 17:14</reference> : There came to him a certain man, kneeling down to him γονυπετων αυτον, falling down at his knees. <div eID="gen2701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2702" type="x-p"/> As to the lifting up or stretching out of the hands, (often joined to kneeling), of which we have seen already several instances, and of which we have a very remarkable one in this book, <reference osisRef="Exo.17.11">Exo 17:11</reference>, where the lifting up or stretching out of the hands of Moses was the means of Israel's prevailing over Amalek; we find many examples of both in ancient authors. Thus Homer: - Εσθλον γαρ Δυ χειρας ανασχεμεν, αι κ' ελεησῃ. <div eID="gen2702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2703" type="x-p"/> Iliad xxiv., ver. 301. <div eID="gen2703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2704" type="x-p"/> For right it is to spread abroad the hands To Jove for mercy. <div eID="gen2704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2705" type="x-p"/> Also Virgil: - <div eID="gen2705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2706" type="x-p"/> Corripio e stratis corpus, <div eID="gen2706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2707" type="x-p"/> Tendoque supinas ad coelum cum voce manus, et munera libo <div eID="gen2707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2708" type="x-p"/> Aeneid iii., ver. 176. <div eID="gen2708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2709" type="x-p"/> I started from my bed, and raised on high <div eID="gen2709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2710" type="x-p"/> My hands and voice in rapture to the sky; <div eID="gen2710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2711" type="x-p"/> And pour libations. <div eID="gen2711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2712" type="x-p"/> Ptt. <div eID="gen2712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2713" type="x-p"/> Dixerat: et Genua Amplexus, genibusque volutans Haerebat. <div eID="gen2713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2714" type="x-p"/> Ibid., ver. 607. <div eID="gen2714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2715" type="x-p"/> Then kneel'd the wretch, and suppliant clung around <div eID="gen2715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2716" type="x-p"/> My knees with tears, and grovell'd on the ground. <div eID="gen2716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2717" type="x-p"/> Id. - media inter numina divum Multa Jovem <div eID="gen2717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2718" type="x-p"/> Manibus Supplex orasse SUPINIS. <div eID="gen2718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2719" type="x-p"/> Ibid. iv., ver. 204. <div eID="gen2719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2720" type="x-p"/> Amidst the statues of the gods he stands, <div eID="gen2720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2721" type="x-p"/> And spreading forth to Jove his lifted hands. <div eID="gen2721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2722" type="x-p"/> Id. <div eID="gen2722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2723" type="x-p"/> Et Duplices cum voce Manus ad sidera <div eID="gen2723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2724" type="x-p"/> Tendit. Ibid. x., ver. 667. <div eID="gen2724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2725" type="x-p"/> And lifted both his hands and voice to heaven. <div eID="gen2725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2726" type="x-p"/> In some cases the person petitioning came forward, and either sat in the dust or kneeled on the ground, placing his left hand on the knee of him from whom he expected the favor, while he touched the person's chin with his right. We have an instance of this also in Homer: Και ρα παροιθ' αυτοιο καθεζετο, και λαβε γουνων Σκαιῃ· δεξιτερῃ δ' αρ' ὑπ' ανθερεωνος ἑλουσα. <div eID="gen2726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2727" type="x-p"/> Iliad i., ver. 500. <div eID="gen2727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2728" type="x-p"/> Suppliant the goddess stood: one hand she placed <div eID="gen2728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2729" type="x-p"/> Beneath his chin, and one his knee embraced. <div eID="gen2729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2730" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen2730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2731" type="x-p"/> When the supplicant could not approach the person to whom he prayed, as where a deity was the object of the prayer, he washed his hands, made an offering, and kneeling down, either stretched out both his hands to heaven, or laid them upon the offering or sacrifice, or upon the altar. Thus Homer represents the priest of Apollo praying: - Χερνιψαντο δ' επειτα, και ουλοχυτας ανελοντο. Τοισιν δε Χρυσης μεγαλ' ευχετο, χειρας ανασχων. <div eID="gen2731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2732" type="x-p"/> Iliad i., ver. 449. <div eID="gen2732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2733" type="x-p"/> With water purify their hands, and take <div eID="gen2733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2734" type="x-p"/> The sacred offering of the salted cake, <div eID="gen2734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2735" type="x-p"/> While thus, with arms devoutly raised in air, <div eID="gen2735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2736" type="x-p"/> And solemn voice, the priest directs his prayer. <div eID="gen2736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2737" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen2737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2738" type="x-p"/> How necessary ablutions of the whole body, and of the hands particularly, accompanied with offerings and sacrifices were, under the law, every reader of the Bible knows: see especially <reference osisRef="Exo.29.1-Exo.29.4">Exo 29:1-4</reference>, where Aaron and his sons were commanded to be washed, previously to their performing the priest's office; and <reference osisRef="Exo.30.19-Exo.30.21">Exo 30:19-21</reference>, where it is said: "Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands - that they die not." See also <reference osisRef="Lev.17.15">Lev 17:15</reference>. When the high priest among the Jews blessed the people, he lifted up his hands, <reference osisRef="Lev.9.22">Lev 9:22</reference>. And the Israelites, when they presented a sacrifice to God, lifted up their hands and placed them on the head of the victim: "If any man of you bring an offering unto the Lord - of the cattle of the herd, and of the flock - he shall put his hand upon the head of the burnt-offering, and it shall be accepted for him, to make atonement for him;" <reference osisRef="Lev.1.2-Lev.1.4">Lev 1:2-4</reference>. To these circumstances the apostle alludes, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1Tim 2:8</reference> : "I will therefore that men pray everywhere, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting." In the apostle's word επαιροντας, lifting up, there is a manifest reference to stretching out the hands to place them either on the altar or on the head of the victim. Four things were signified by this lifting up of the hands. 1. It was the posture of supplication, and expressed a strong invitation - Come to my help; 2. It expressed the earnest desire of the person to lay hold on the help he required, by bringing him who was the object of his prayer to his assistance; 3. It showed the ardor of the person to receive the blessings he expected; and 4. By this act he designated and consecrated his offering or sacrifice to his God. <div eID="gen2738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2739" type="x-p"/> From a great number of evidences and coincidences it is not unreasonable to conclude that the heathens borrowed all that was pure and rational, even in their mode of worship, from the ancient people of God; and that the preceding quotations are proofs of this.
entries.e76f490a8ccca9ed94995eb341286e0757b54b8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen2739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2740" type="x-p"/> The flax and the barley was smitten - The word פשתה pishtah, flax, Mr. Parkhurst thinks, is derived from the root פשט pashat, to strip, because the substance which we term flax is properly the bark or rind of the vegetable, pilled or stripped off the stalks. From time immemorial Egypt was celebrated for the production and manufacture of flax: hence the linen and fine linen of Egypt, so often spoken of in ancient authors. <div eID="gen2740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2741" type="x-p"/> Barley - שערה seorah, from שער saar, to stand on end, to be rough, bristly, etc.; hence שער sear, the hair of the head, and שעיר sair, a he-goat, because of its shaggy hair; and hence also barley, because of the rough and prickly beard with which the ears are covered and defended. <div eID="gen2741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2742" type="x-p"/> Dr. Pocock has observed that there is a double seed-time and harvest in Egypt: Rice, India wheat, and a grain called the corn of Damascus, and in Italian surgo rosso, are sown and reaped at a very different time from wheat, barley and flax. The first are sown in March, before the overflowing of the Nile, and reaped about October; whereas the wheat and barley are sown in November and December, as soon as the Nile is gone off, and are reaped before May. <div eID="gen2742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2743" type="x-p"/> Pliny observes, Hist. Nat., lib. xviii., cap. 10, that in Egypt the barley is ready for reaping in six months after it is sown, and wheat in seven. In Aegypto Hordeum sexto a satu mense, Feumenta septimo metuntur. <div eID="gen2743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2744" type="x-p"/> The flax was boiled - Meaning, I suppose, was grown up into a stalk: the original is גבעל gibol, podded or was in the pod. <div eID="gen2744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2745" type="x-p"/> The word well expresses that globous pod on the top of the stalk of flax which succeeds the flower and contains the seed, very properly expressed by the Septuagint, το δε λινον σπερματιζον, but the flax was in seed or was seeding.
entries.e9100cc844e6f0e245392b4e74f58741351c57d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen2745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2746" type="x-p"/> But the wheat and the rye were not smitten - Wheat, חטה chittah, which Mr. Parkhurst thinks should be derived from the Chaldee and Samaritan חטי chati, which signifies tender, delicious, delicate, because of the superiority of its flavor, etc., to every other kind of grain. But this term in Scripture appears to mean any kind of bread-corn. Rye, כסמת cussemeth, from כסם casam, to have long hair; and hence, though the particular species is not known, the word must mean some bearded grain. The Septuagint call it ολυρα, the Vulgate for, and Aquila ζεα, which signify the grain called spelt; and some suppose that rice is meant. <div eID="gen2746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2747" type="x-p"/> Mr. Harmer, referring to the double harvest in Egypt mentioned by Dr. Pocock, says that the circumstance of the wheat and the rye being אפילת aphiloth, dark or hidden, as the margin renders it, (i.e., they were sown, but not grown up), shows that it was the Indian wheat or surgo rosso mentioned <reference osisRef="Exo.9.31">Exo 9:31</reference>, which, with the rye, escaped, while the barley and flax were smitten because they were at or nearly at a state of maturity. See Harmer's Obs., vol. iv., p. 11, edit 1808. But what is intended by the words in the Hebrew text we cannot positively say, as there is a great variety of opinions on this subject, both among the versions and the commentators. The Anglo-Saxon translator, probably from not knowing the meaning of the words, omits the whole verse.
entries.4a8186bf6b1615156825fb6b8dccde763f628f3e: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen2747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2748" type="x-p"/> Spread abroad his hands - Probably with the rod of God in them. See what has been said on the spreading out of the hands in prayer, <reference osisRef="Exo.9.29">Exo 9:29</reference>. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.9.29">Exo 9:29</reference> (note).
entries.a1e3749012303edfd01abbc4bdd083f703d9e26d: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen2748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2749" type="x-p"/> He sinned yet more, and hardened his heart - These were merely acts of his own; "for who can deny," says Mr. Psalmanazar, "that what God did on Pharaoh was much more proper to soften than to harden his heart; especially when it is observable that it was not till after seeing each miracle, and after the ceasing of each plague, that his heart is said to have been hardened? The verbs here used are in the conjugations pihel and hiphil, and often signify a bare permission, from which it is plain that the words should have been read, God suffered the heart of Pharaoh to be hardened." - Universal Hist., vol. i., p. 494. Note D.
entries.190f27fdff7cf49469aa5250e55b5302fdcd0db5: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen2749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2750" type="x-p"/> And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened - In consequence of his sinning yet more, and hardening his own heart against both the judgments and mercies of God, we need not be surprised that, after God had given him the means of softening and repentance, and he had in every instance resisted and abused them, he should at last have been left to the hardness and darkness of his own obstinate heart, so as to fill up the measure of his iniquity, and rush headlong to his own destruction. <div eID="gen2750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2751" type="x-p"/> In the fifth, sixth, and seventh plagues described in this chapter, we have additional proofs of the justice and mercy of God, as well as of the stupidity, rebellion, and wickedness of Pharaoh and his courtiers. As these continued to contradict and resist, it was just that God should continue to inflict those punishments which their iniquities deserved. Yet in the midst of judgment he remembers mercy; and therefore Moses and Aaron are sent to inform the Egyptians that such plagues would come if they continued obstinate. Here is mercy; the cattle only are destroyed, and the people saved! Is it not evident from all these messages, and the repeated expostulations of Moses and Aaron in the name and on the authority of God, that Pharaoh was bound by no fatal necessity to continue his obstinacy; that he might have humbled himself before God, and thus prevented the disasters that fell on the land, and saved himself and his people from destruction? But he would sin, and therefore he must be punished. <div eID="gen2751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2752" type="x-p"/> In the sixth plague Pharaoh had advantages which he had not before. The magicians, by their successful imitations of the miracles wrought by Moses, made it doubtful to the Egyptians whether Moses himself was not a magician acting without any Divine authority; but the plague of the boils, which they could not imitate, by which they were themselves afflicted, and which they confessed to be the finger of God, decided the business. <div eID="gen2752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2753" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh had no longer any excuse, and must know that he had now to contend, not with Moses and Aaron, mortals like himself, but with the living God. How strange, then, that he should continue to resist! Many affect to be astonished at this, and think it must be attributed only to a sovereign controlling influence of God, which rendered it impossible for him to repent or take warning. But the whole conduct of God shows the improbability of this opinion: and is not the conduct of Pharaoh and his courtiers copied and reacted by thousands who are never suspected to be under any such necessitating decree? Every sinner under heaven, who has the Bible in his hand, is acting the same part. God says to the swearer and the profane, Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain; and yet common swearing and profaneness are most scandalously common among multitudes who bear the Christian name, and who presume on the mercy of God to get at last to the kingdom of heaven! He says also, Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy; thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not steal; thou shalt not bear false witness; thou shalt not covet; and sanctions all these commandments with the most awful penalties: and yet, with all these things before them, and the professed belief that they came from God, Sabbath-breakers, men-slayers, adulterers, fornicators, thieves, dishonest men, false witnesses, liars, slanderers, backbiters, covetous men, lovers of the world more than lovers of God, are found by hundreds and thousands! What were the crimes of the poor half-blind Egyptian king when compared with these! He sinned against a comparatively unknown God; these sin against the God of their fathers - against the God and Father of Him whom they call their Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ! They sin with the Bible in their hand, and a conviction of its Divine authority in their hearts. They sin against light and knowledge; against the checks of their consciences, the reproofs of their friends, the admonitions of the messengers of God; against Moses and Aaron in the law; against the testimony of all the prophets; against the evangelists, the apostles, the Maker of heaven and earth, the Judge of all men, and the Savior of the world! What were Pharaoh's crimes to the crimes of these? On comparison, his atom of moral turpitude is lost in their world of iniquity. And yet who supposes these to be under any necessitating decree to sin on, and go to perdition? Nor are they; nor was Pharaoh. In all things God has proved both his justice and mercy to be clear in this point.
